list.listitem: Labor is a natural process for which selected medical intervention can reduce maternal morbidity and improve fetal outcomes. A
Routine external fetal monitoring in labor has no benefit in terms of neonatal outcome. A

Epidural analgesia in labor is safe and is not associated with an increase in cesarean section rates; however, it may cause longer second stage of labor, more frequent need for oxytocin augmentation, higher rates of instrumented delivery, fever, and hypotension during labor. A
Routine episiotomy is not recommended due to increased rates of third- and fourth-degree perineal trauma and no evidence to support decreased rates of subsequent organ prolapse and/or incontinence. B
Oxytocin augmentation is safe and effective as a management option for arrested labor. B
There were just over 3.6 million births in the United States in 2020, which is down 4% from 2019 and the lowest since 1980. (see chapter on prenatal care).
According to the American Academy of Family Physicians 2017 Practice Profile Survey, 19% of the 2700 respondents reported delivering one or more babies.

In a retrospective cohort study of 2000 low-risk women managed in labor by family physicians and 2865 low-risk women managed by obstetricians, women managed by family physicians were less likely to have their labors induced (10.4% vs. 8.6%), receive oxytocin augmentation (17.8% vs. 14.9%), have epidural anesthesia (17.0% vs. 5.4%), have episiotomies (74.5% vs. 53.7%), or have cesarean sections (16.0% vs. 9.3%). There were no differences in neonatal complication rates.

Outcomes with respect to perinatal mortality and adverse maternal outcomes were similar for deliveries performed by family physicians and obstetricians based on a retrospective population-based hospital birth cohort study of 859,180 Canadian (except Quebec) infants who were more than 20 weeks gestational age and at a birth weight greater than 500 g.
This chapter will address labor and delivery for women presenting at term in labor with a singleton gestation.

Uterine contractions leading to progressive cervical change. Active labor can be defined as regular uterine contractions that are causing cervical effacement and dilation and the cervix is at least 6 cm dilated. This is based on updated information on normal labor curves of more than 60,000 spontaneous vaginal singleton deliveries. Labor can be divided into three stages: Stage 1 onset of labor through complete cervical dilation; Stage 2 start of maternal pushing to delivery of the infant; Stage 3 after delivery of infant to delivery of placenta.
The definition of active labor has changed from 4cm dilation to 6cm dilation based on substantial evidence that rate of dilation is variable until that point.

Fetal presentation (eg, vertex, breech) should be confirmed upon hospital admission. Confirmation by ultrasound is more accurate than clinical examination; clinical examination can miss up to 30% of non-cephalic presentations. During prenatal care, fetal presentation should be determined at 36 weeks by ultrasound so that external cephalic version can be offered.

However, authors of a meta-analysis of 4 RCTs found that use of sonographic assessment of fetal occiput position during second stage labor compared with digital examination did not decrease rates of cesarean delivery or sequential use of different instruments for operative vaginal delivery. Use of manual rotation of occiput posterior or transverse positions during labor at term modestly increases the rate of spontaneous vaginal delivery (65% vs 60%; relative risk 1.09, 95% CI 1.03 - 1.16) and decreases the use of episiotomy, based on 7 RCTs including 1402 patients. Cesarean deliveries and neonatal outcomes were not different.

In a cohort study of more than 11,000 consecutive singleton deliveries in Finland, cephalic malpresentations occurred in 5.4% (persistent occipitoposterior 5.2%, face 0.1%, brow 0.14%), 3.1% had breech presentation, and 0.12% a transverse lie. The OR for cesarean section were 14.89 (95% CI, 11.91-18.63) in breech presentation and 4.57 (95% CI, 3.85-5.42) in persistent occipitoposterior presentation.

In cases, where breech presentation is confirmed in labor or with spontaneous rupture of membranes, caesarean delivery is indicated because despite a slight increase in maternal morbidity, there is a decrease in short-term neonatal morbidity and mortality (see chapter Breech delivery).

Risk assessment is performed for women in active labor and includes initial fetal heart rate assessment, prenatal risk review, and risk in labor assessment to identify women who may require additional intervention.

High-risk situations include abnormal fetal heart rate; bleeding; breech presentation or multiple gestation; dysfunctional labor; fetal risk such as congenital heart disease; growth restriction or oligohydramnios; maternal chronic disease such as hypertension, diabetes, or lupus; oxytocin use; postdate pregnancy (>42 weeks' gestation), or thick meconium.

section.type: Cervical Examination to Monitor Labor Progress
section.heading: Cervical Examination to Monitor Labor Progress

list.listitem: There is no clinical evidence evaluating the optimal frequency of cervical examination to monitor labor progress. Often, examination frequency is determined by a combination of factors which consider fetal and maternal status, staffing models, and hospital protocols/standards of care.

Despite an absence of clinical trial evidence, it is standard practice in many settings to minimize the number of cervical examinations to potentially reduce the risk of chorioamnionitis and subsequent neonatal sepsis.

However, the ICSI guideline suggests frequent cervical checks (every 1-2 hours) to assess labor progress, noting that the Frigoletto et al. trial on active management of labor used hourly checks in their protocol.

section.type: Monitoring Fetal Well being During Labor
section.heading: Monitoring Fetal Well being During Labor

list.listitem: External fetal monitoring as a routine practice does not decrease neonatal morbidity or mortality compared with intermittent auscultation. Nurse auscultatory monitoring with a DeLee stethoscope or Doppler ultrasound in these studies is done during a contraction and for 30 seconds after the contraction every 30 minutes during active labor and every 15 minutes during stage 2.

Use of a partograph (pre-printed form providing a pictorial overview of labor progress) is of uncertain benefit over no partograph on cesarean section rates, labor augmentation, or APGAR scores based on a Cochrane review of 3 trials. There were also no clear differences in outcomes when using a 2-hour vs. 4-hour action line. As noted below, women’s labors are highly variable and crossing the alert line on the partograph is common (49% in this study) and did not predict severe adverse outcomes.

Continuous fetal monitoring has no demonstrated benefit in improving overall perinatal death rate over intermittent auscultation but is associated with half the rate of neonatal seizures (although no difference in cerebral palsy or infant mortality); however, it is associated with an increase in cesarean section and instrumented delivery rates.
Continuous fetal heart rate monitoring is recommended for women with high-risk conditions. C
A three-tiered system for categorization of fetal heart rate tracing is recommended; however, intra- and interobserver varbiability is high.

One study comparing sonographic assessment of amniotic fluid index (AFI) on admission versus no sonographic assessment of AFI on admission found a higher incidence of fetal distress and labor augmentation for those in the intervention group but no differences in newborn outcomes.
Technology employed to confirm the presence of fetal distress such as scalp pH and fetal pulse oximetry does not decrease cesarean-section rates or improve neonatal outcomes.

Despite an absence of clinical trial evidence, it is standard practice in most settings to place internal scalp electrodes and intrauterine pressure catheters when there is concern for fetal well-being demonstrated on external monitoring.
The following interventions can improve fetal oxygenation: maternal lateral positioning, oxygen supplementation, and intravenous fluid bolus. B

Employing a trained doula/labor coach can be helpful. A Cochrane review of 26 trials with more than 15,800 women found that women with continuous labor support were more likely to have a spontaneous vaginal birth (RR 1.08; 95% CI, 1.04-1.12), shorter labors (mean difference –0.68 hours; 95% CI, –1.04 to –0.34), fewer caesarean sections (RR 0.75; 95% CI, 0.64-0.88) or instrumental vaginal birth (RR 0.90; 95% CI, 0.85-0.96), and less likely to have intrapartum analgesia. In addition, supported women were less likely to have a baby with a low 5-minute Apgar score (RR 0.62; 95% CI, 0.46-0.85).

In a single-blinded RCT of 80 primigravid women in spontaneous labor at term, use of a specific sequence of nonpharmacological interventions—Swiss ball exercises, lumbosacral massage, and a warm shower—applied at specific points during cervical dilatation significantly reduced pain, delayed and reduced requests for pharmacological analgesia, and shortened duration of labor by 72 minutes.

Cochrane authors found supporting evidence for water immersion, relaxation, acupuncture, massage, and local anesthetic nerve blocks for labor pain with few adverse effects. Relaxation was associated with fewer assisted vaginal births and acupuncture was associated with fewer assisted vaginal births and cesarean sections.

Intravenous (IV) or intramuscular (IM) narcotics (eg, hydromorphone 1-4 mg IM every 4-6 hours, morphine sulfate 2-10 mg IV/IM every 2-6 hours) are an option for labor analgesia. In clinical practice, there is a theoretical concern that cross-placental passage of these agents will result in neonatal respiratory suppression if given in close proximity to the delivery. There is no evidence demonstrating neonatal risk to substantiate this concern if a narcotic is administered within 2 to 4 hours of delivery and naltrexone is available in the delivery room.
Epidural analgesia is considered safe in most settings and for most women in labor. In the absence of contraindications, ACOG states neuraxial anesthesia can be offered at any stage of labor.
Epidural use is associated with increased risk of intrapartum fever, which may lead to a neonatal sepsis evaluation.However, epidural use is not associated with an increased rate of neonatal sepsis.

Despite some controversy, the most recent systematic review of 14 RCTs did not find an association between epidural use and cesarean-section rate.However, patients with an epidural have a longer second stage of labor, more frequent need for oxytocin augmentation, higher rates of instrumented delivery, fever, and hypotension during labor.

A retrospective study of more than 40,000 vaginal singleton deliveries found that epidural use increased the length of second-stage labor in both nulliparous and multiparous women. For nulliparous women, the median length of the second stage increased from 47 to 112 minutes while the 95th percentile increase went from 190 to 302 minutes. For multiparous women, the length increased from 14 to 38 minutes on average while the upper limit of normal increased from 79 to 217 minutes with epidural use.

An RCT done at a university and a non-university hospital compared routine epidural analgesia to epidural analgesia by request. They found that routine epidural analgesia led to more operative deliveries and maternal complications including hypotension and motor blockade compared to analgesia by request. They concluded that routine use of epidural analgesia cannot be supported based on their study results.

Intrathecal fentanyl followed by epidural bupivacaine plus fentanyl (if needed for pain relief) was more effective than systemic hydromorphone (1 mg IV plus 1 mg IM, twice) and did not increase the cesarean delivery rate. Common side effects are hypotension, loss of bladder control necessitating urinary bladder catheterization, back pain, and postepidural headache.

In a small RCT from Australia, fentanyl given subcutaneously or intranasally was as effective as intramuscular pethidine in relieving labor pain, but offered greater patient satisfaction, less sedation, shorter labor, fewer nursery admissions, and fewer breastfeeding difficulties.

Inhaled nitrous oxide (through patient self-administration) can be used in the first and second stages of labor, and has been used more extensively in the UK and Australia, with more recent use in the United States. It is less effective compared to epidural for reduction in pain scores, but has the advantage of not limiting mobility. Side effects include nausea, dizziness, and drowsiness.

Pudendal nerve blocks may be useful as an alternative to systemic narcotics or epidural analgesia. These are most useful when applied in the second and sometimes third stages of labor. No evidence exists that compares this method in terms of outcomes to the other, more commonly used methods of labor analgesia.

One study found that cutaneous water injections (4 injections of 0.5 cc sterile water subcutaneously) during the first stage of labor can bring pain relief to select women with severe low back pain in labor.
In one small RCT, there was no benefit of acupuncture over sham acupuncture for pain relief during induced labor.

There is insufficient evidence to determine whether or not hypnosis, biofeedback, sterile water injection, aromatherapy, TENS, or parenteral opioids are more effective than placebo or other interventions.

In one large RCT of 1067 women, randomization to walking during labor versus bed rest conferred neither benefit nor harm. Because the cesarean section rate was already very low for the control group (6% vs. 4% for the intervention group), it would be difficult for walking to demonstrate improvement.
The ICSI guideline supports appropriate comfort measures including oral fluids, fluid balance maintenance, position changes, back rubs, music, ambulation, and tub bath/shower.

Immersion in water during the first stage may decrease pain and shorten labor duration. There were no differences in mode of delivery and data were insufficient to determine differences in neonatal outcomes such as infection rates.
IV hydration has been demonstrated to potentially decrease need for augmentation with oxytocin for nulliparous women in labor.
Some institutions limit oral food and fluid intake in labor due to concerns about anesthesia complications should general anesthesia become necessary.

Per the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) Committee opinion, women with uncomplicated labor and uncomplicated patients with planned cesarean delivery should be allowed modest amounts of liquids orally during labor.
Data do not support routine use of prophylactic drugs for reducing gastric aspiration (eg, antacids, H2 receptor antagonists) in normal labor.
When given the freedom to do so, women frequently change position in labor.

Amniotomy (deliberate rupture of the fetal membranes) is performed prior to placement of fetal scalp electrodes, fetal blood sampling, and to assess for the presence of meconium. There is evidence to support that this procedure can shorten labor by 1 to 2 hours, but the procedure has risks including cord prolapse, increased uterine forces accompanied by increased pain or fetal distress, and the potential for infection.
Data do not support use of amniotomy for routinely shortening labor, but it is recommended by ACOG for patients undergoing augmentation or induction of labor.
Active management of labor does not reduce the rate of cesarean delivery but may decrease the length of labor and increase patient satisfaction in nulliparas.

When used for induction or augmentation of labor, it is unclear whether discontinuing oxytocin at the onset of active labor leads to reduced rates of cesarean delivery. The active phase of labor was 30 minutes longer but neonatal outcomes were equivalent in a 2025 meta-analysis.

Prolonged latent phase should not be an indication for cesarean section because most women will reach the active phase of labor with expectant management OR with amniotomy with or without oxytocin infusion.

In a study of abnormal progress in labor and adverse outcomes, investigators found that 49% of 9995 women in spontaneous labor presenting at 6 or fewer cm dilation crossed the alert line on the partograph (<1 cm dilation per hour) and 2.2% had severe adverse outcomes but crossing the alert line did not predict those outcomes.

Based on the work of the Consortium on Safe Labor, active phase likely begins at 6 cm based on when the rate of cervical change accelerates. Prior to 6 cm nulliparous and multiparous women dilate at about the same rate. This definition has been codified by ACOG in its 2024 practice recommendation on management of the first and second stages of labor.

This is different than previous knowledge based on Friedman's work in the 1950s and 60s. Furthermore, the rate of cervical change in the active phase is likely slower in modern women. The 95th percentile or upper limit of normal for nulliparous women was 1.0 to 1.5 cm over 2 hours and for multiparous women was 1 to 3 cm over 2 hours.

In a before and after study at a single institution, implementing ACOG consensus recommendations for prevention of primary cesarean section significantly reduced cesarean-section rates. Included in the study were 3283 before and 3068 women after with singleton pregnancies at term, in vertex presentation, in spontaneous or induced labor, and with epidural anesthesia. Cesarean-section rates decreased from 9.4% to 6.9% (OR 0.71; 95% CI 0.59-0.85). Changes in protocol for labor management were defining active labor as >6 cm vs. 4 cm, defining first-stage labor arrest to no change after 4 hours of adequate or 6 hours of inadequate contractions in women with an epidural, and defining second-stage arrest of labor to no progress for ≥4 hours in nulliparas or 3 hours in multiparas with an epidural.

Based on a study of more than 40,000 vaginal singleton deliveries, the length of the second stage is likely longer than previously thought. Also as noted above, epidural use increases the length of this stage.

An absolute maximum length of the second stage has not been established.As long as maternal and fetal conditions permit, allow for at least 3-4 hours of pushing for a nulliparous woman and at least 2-3 hours of pushing in a multiparous woman before diagnosing arrest of descent. Longer duration of pushing may be appropriate per individual patient.
ACOG recommends pushing begin when dilation is complete. An umbrella review of meta-analyses found no difference in maternal or neonatal outcomes with "laboring down" compared with immediate pushing.

Maternal positions during second stage include upright or supine. Authors of a Cochrane review of 32 low to moderate-quality trials found that upright positions were associated with a possible shorter second stage (MD −6.16 minutes; 95% CI, −9.74 to −2.59 minutes), a reduction in assisted deliveries (RR 0.75; 95% CI, 0.66 to 0.86); and a reduction in episiotomies (average RR 0.75; 95% CI, 0.61 to 0.92), but no clear difference in rates of cesarean section or third- or fourth-degree perineal tears. With respect to newborn outcomes, upright positions were associated with fewer abnormal fetal heart rate patterns (RR 0.46; 95% CI, 0.22 to 0.93), but no clear difference in the number of infants admitted to neonatal intensive care.

For nulliparous women receiving neuraxial anesthesia, data support pushing at the start of the second stage of labor. Potential risks of delayed pushing include infection, hemorrhage, and neonatal acidemia. In a meta-analysis of 12 RCTs, there were no significant differences in mode of delivery between delayed and immediate pushing groups.

The benefit of coached pushing (Valsalva-type against a closed glottis) in stage 2 labor is unclear. In one study of women who were not receiving epidural analgesia or oxytocin, coached pushing reduced pushing time by 15 minutes (46 minutes vs. 59 minutes), and in another study, spontaneous pushing resulted in shorter second stage (41 minutes vs. 50 minutes) and greater patient satisfaction.

Immersion in water during the second stage should be considered experimental as it has not shown maternal or fetal benefits and there have been case reports of rare but serious adverse events in newborns.

Warm packs applied to the perineum starting in late second-stage labor reduced the risk of third- and fourth-degree perineal lacerations (ARR 4.5; NNT 22), reduced pain during childbirth, and may reduce postpartum urinary incontinence.

Episiotomy (incision of the perineum) likely causes an increase in severe lacerations to the perineum without reducing urinary incontinence or dyspareunia. There are no data to support its use to prevent pelvic relaxation. Authors of a Cochrane review of eight RCTs found that for women where an unassisted vaginal birth was anticipated, use of selective episiotomy may result in 30% fewer women experiencing severe perineal/vaginal trauma (RR 0.70; 95% CI, 0.52-0.94). Routine episiotomy is no longer a standard procedure in most clinical settings.

If episiotomy is needed, mediolateral is preferred over midline because of the increased risk of anal sphincter lacerations with midline episiotomy. However mediolateral episiotomy may be associated with increased risk of perineal pain and dyspareunia. B
Low quality evidence suggests vacuum extraction can assist with successful occiput posterior deliveries.
Perineal massage during the second stage of labor can also reduce the risk of third- and fourth-degree lacerations. B

Continuous perineal suture is preferred over interrupted suture for second-degree lacerations. Surgical glue or suture can be used for first-degree lacerations or skin repair of second-degree lacerations. B

Active management of stage 3, defined as administration of a prophylactic uterotonic drug (eg, oxytocin) after delivery of the anterior shoulder, followed by immediate clamping and cutting the cord, then followed by delivery of the placenta by controlled cord traction or maternal pushing, is associated with reduced postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) (ARR 9.7%; NNT 10 to prevent 1 PPH).

Authors of a Cochrane review of 8 trials with 8892 women confirmed a lower rate of significant PPH, but note that the quality of evidence is poor and there was a higher risk of elevated maternal diastolic blood pressure, vomiting after birth, after-pains, use of analgesia from birth to discharge, and return to the hospital with bleeding. While there was no increased risk of neonatal care unit admission, there was a decrease in the baby's birth weight with active management, likely due to lower blood volume from interference with placental transfusion.

Delayed cord clamping for term infants results in higher mean birth weights and higher hemoglobin and iron stores; conversely, fewer infants in early cord clamping groups require phototherapy for jaundice. As it benefits most newborns, delayed cord clamping of 30-60 seconds in vigorous newborns is recommended.

Among preterm infants, Cochrane authors found that delayed cord clamping for 30 to 120 seconds vs. early clamping appears to be associated with less need for transfusion, better circulatory stability, less intraventricular hemorrhage (all grades), and lower risk for necrotizing enterocolitis.
Oxytocin is most commonly administered IM in a dose of 10 units or IV as 20 units mixed with either normal saline or lactated ringer solution to increase uterine tone and minimize bleeding.

Oral misoprostol (400-600 µg) has been used in several studies to prevent PPH. In one study, misoprostol performed as well as oxytocin but, in the other study, PPH (blood loss >1000 mL) occurred more often (NNTH 89). There were no differences in need for transfusion or admission to intensive care in either study.

Ergot alkaloids can also be used prophylactically in stage 3 labor to reduce PPH, but side effects including elevation of blood pressure and more pain after birth requiring analgesia limit their usefulness.
Fetal distress can be defined by presence of fetal heart rate abnormalities in labor and/or presence of meconium-stained amniotic fluid.

Fetal heart rate abnormalities requiring evaluation and continued surveillance include fetal tachycardia (>160 beats per minute); marked variability; absent variability without decelerations; fetal bradycardia (<110 without absent variability); absence of accelerations after fetal stimulation; or decelerations that are 2 to 9 minutes, recurrent late but with moderate variability, or recurrent variable with minimal or moderate variability.

Prompt evaluation and management are indicated for absent fetal heart rate variability and any of: recurrent late decelerations, recurrent variable decelerations, fetal bradycardia (<110), or sinusoidal pattern. Management may include maternal position change, maternal oxygen, administration of a fluid bolus, discontinuation of labor stimulus, assessment of maternal hypotension or uterine tachysystole, checking for cord prolapse or rapid cervical dilation or fetal descent, treatment of underlying conditions, amnioinfusion, consideration of obstetric consultation, and expedited delivery.

Administration of maternal oxygen in the setting of fetal heart rate abnormalities indicative of distress, including tachycardia, late decelerations, and sinusoidal patterns, is thought to be helpful, although there is insufficient evidence to evaluate the impact of this intervention on improved neonatal outcomes.

Amnioinfusion is associated with improvement in perinatal outcome. When variable fetal heart rate decelerations are present, amnioinfusion to minimize the potential for cord compression reduces occurrence of variable fetal heart rate decelerations. Amnioinfusion is recommended for repetitive severe variable late decelerations or prolonged decelerations, but not for thick meconium.
Amnioinfusion for repetitive variable fetal heart rate decelerations may safely reduce the rate of cesarean delivery.

Administration of a tocolytic agent such as a betamimetic can improve fetal heart rate tracings and decrease uterine activity. There is, however, a lack of evidence to support this as beneficial in terms of clinically important outcomes and one small RCT found that prophylactic betamimetic therapy conferred no benefits and was associated with an increase in forceps deliveries.

When fetal distress occurs and persists despite interventions to improve uteroplacental blood flow and oxygen transport to the fetus (eg, maternal position changes, IV fluids, tocolytic agents, and maternal oxygen administration), it is standard practice in most settings to move to an operative or assisted delivery. There are no clinical trials comparing operative versus conservative management of suspected fetal distress.
Walking to augment latent labor contractions is commonly employed. Although there is no harm associated with this intervention, there is also no advantage in terms of labor progress.

Lack of progress in cervical dilation for 2 hours during the active phase of labor does not by itself appear to be sufficient rationale to indicate cesarean delivery given the favorable neonatal outcomes associated with vaginal delivery.

If maternal and fetal conditions allow, then 24 hours or more should be allowed for the latent phase and 12 to 18 hours of oxytocin administration given after the rupture of membranes before diagnosing failed induction of labor.

Arrest of dilation or active-phase arrest should not be diagnosed until a woman has achieved 6 cm or greater with ruptured membranes and no cervical change after 4 hours of adequate contractions as determined by intrauterine pressure catheter (200 Montevideo units [MVU]/10 minutes) OR has reached 6 cm or greater with ruptured membranes and no cervical change after 6 hours of oxytocin infusion and inadequate contractions based on MVUs as above.
For cases of fetal malposition, manual rotation of the fetal occiput in the second stage of labor is a reasonable intervention to consider before operative delivery.

For cases of arrest of descent, operative vaginal delivery in the second stage of labor by experienced and well-trained physicians should be considered a safe and acceptable alternative to cesarean delivery.
Hypocontractility is a common cause of protracted labor; options for management include IV fluids (150 cc/hour), discontinuing or reducing epidural anesthesia, and/or use of oxytocin augmentation.
Labor in water in one study was as effective as amniotomy with or without oxytocin with respect to time to delivery (10½ hours in both groups) with less pain and higher patient satisfaction.
Oxytocin use in the setting of arrested labor is safe and effective to facilitate continued labor progression.
Amniotomy is a common clinical practice to augment stage 2 labor in multigravida patients. Data do not strongly support use of amniotomy for this purpose.

Authors of a Cochrane review of prevention trials found early amniotomy together with oxytocin augmentation was associated with a shortened duration of the first stage of labor (approximately one hour) and a modest reduction in cesarean birth rates when compared with expectant management (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.77 to 0.99; 11 trials; 7753 patients).
Active management of labor, early amniotomy with oxytocin augmentation, has not been shown to reduce cesarean-section rate for low-risk nulliparous women.

Vacuum-assisted delivery does not have a higher risk for intracranial hemorrhage, but does have a lower risk of permanent nerve injury compared with forceps-assisted delivery. One study found use of the Kiwi Omnicup to be more likely to result in a failed vacuum delivery than conventional cups.

Forceps delivery is associated with higher maternal morbidity than vacuum-assisted delivery (eg, cesarean-sections, maternal trauma), but decreased neonatal morbidity in terms of reduced cephalohematoma and retinal hemorrhage.

Authors of a Cochrane review of instruments for assisted vaginal birth suggest, with low certainty evidence, that use of forceps may have higher rates of successful vaginal delivery than vacuum cups, but with a higher rate of perineal trauma and increased pain requirements.

One study (ANODE trial) demonstrated that administration of a single-dose antibiotic after operative vaginal delivery may reduce risk for postpartum infection. However, this is not currently recommended by the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, citing that this study was done in the United Kingdom, and 89% of the women received an episiotomy. Therefore, it would be reasonable to consider antibiotics in the case of an operative vaginal delivery and episiotomy.
Cesarean section does not protect women from pelvic organ prolapse.
Group B streptococcus (GBS)—routine screening of all patients is recommended between 35 and 37 weeks' gestation (see chapter on prenatal care).

Pregnant women who delivered a previous child with early-onset invasive GBS, had an episode of GBS bacteriuria during the current pregnancy, present in labor prior to 37 weeks' gestation (unless a negative GBS swab is documented within the past 6 weeks), or have a positive GBS culture should be treated in labor.

The preferred treatment is penicillin G, 5 million units IV initially, followed by 2.5 million units IV every 4 hours until delivery. Alternatives include ampicillin 2 g IV initially, followed by 1 g IV every 4 hours until delivery. For penicillin-allergic patients, when the organism is not known to be clindamycin resistant, clindamycin 900 mg IV every 8 hours until delivery is a good alternative.
In patients with a combination of clindamycin resistance and severe penicillin allergy, vancomycin 1 g IV every 12 hours could be considered.
Chorioamnionitis is diagnosed based on clinical criteria; treatment is outlined in the chapter on postpartum hemorrhage and includes IV antibiotics and rapid delivery.
Determining the cause of PPH is important to facilitate appropriate management decisions. Common causes of PPH are listed and management is discussed in the chapter on postpartum hemorrhage.
Prevention efforts include administration of uterotonic agents, controlled cord traction, and uterine massage after placental delivery, as appropriate.
Occurs unpredictably. Clinicians should be aware of risk factors, however, most cases occur in normal-sized infants of non-diabetic mothers.

Elective cesarean delivery may be considered to prevent shoulder dystocia when the estimated fetal weight is greater than 5000 g in a woman without gestational diabetes or greater than 4500 g in women with or without gestational diabetes. C

Management options for shoulder dystocia vary depending on the clinical situation. Maneuvers to open the pelvic outlet are generally helpful (eg, McRoberts maneuver, Wood's Screw maneuver). Changing delivery position from a lithotomy position to a hand/knee position and delivering the posterior shoulder is also often helpful. More recent data suggest that delivery of the posterior arm is highly in successful in accomplishing delivery.

list.listitem: Maternal fever >100.4°F (must be present for diagnosis) plus at least 2 of the following clinical criteria: Fetal tachycardia (HR >160 bpm x 5 minutes) Maternal tachycardia (HR >100 bpm x 5 minutes) Uterine tenderness Foul-smelling or purulent amniotic fluid Maternal leukocytosis (WBC count >2 standard deviations above the mean)

Despite clinical criteria being present, histologic evidence is only present in a small percentage of cases; in 1 study, histologic confirmation was present in only 38.1% of cases diagnosed clinically

IV antibiotics; commonly used options include: Ampicillin and gentamicin—ampicillin 2 g every 6 hours and gentamicin 2 mg/kg loading dose then 1.5 mg/kg every 8 hours OR single dose of 4 to 7 mg/kg gentamicin once daily Piperacillin/tazobactam (Zosyn)—piperacillin 3.375 g every 6 hours and tazobactam 1.5 g every 6 hours Cefazolin (Ancef) and gentamicin—cefazolin 1 g every 8 hours and gentamicin 2 mg/kg loading dose then 1.5 mg/kg gentamicin every 8 hours OR single dose of 5.1 mg/kg gentamicin once daily
Delivery treats the infection; however, chorioamnionitis itself is not an indication for immediate cesarean section

feature.caption: Common Causes of Postpartum Hemorrhage.
feature.feature_body:
Uterine atony Cervical laceration Use of episiotomy (midline or mediolateral) Instrumented (assisted) vaginal delivery Retained placental products Includes abnormal placentation: accreta, increta, percreta
Uterine inversion or rupture Coagulopathy: DIC, HELLP syndrome (see chapter on Preeclampsia) Subinvolution of uterus Retained products of conception Endometritis Hereditary coagulopathy Abbreviations: DIC, diffuse intravascular coagulation; HELLP, hemolysis, elevated liver function, low platelets.
